name: TRAPPIST-1
source: NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP: Planetary Systems Composite Parameters (pscomppars) for measured values and their per-parameter references, Planetary Systems table (ps, default_flag=1) for each planet's default parameter set; cross-checked against Gaia DR3, SIMBAD and Agol et al. 2021. Built by tools/pipeline/exoplanets.py.

exoplanetCount.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP: select count(*) from pscomppars (one row per confirmed planet)

teffK.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (st_teff); Agol et al. 2021

radiusSun.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (st_rad); Agol et al. 2021

massSun.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (st_mass); Agol et al. 2021
massSun.note: Agol et al. 2021 adopt this mass from the Mann et al. (2019) M_Ks-mass relation.

luminosityLogSun.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (st_lum); Agol et al. 2021

luminositySun.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (10^st_lum); Agol et al. 2021
luminositySun.note: Linear form of luminosityLogSun. Agol et al. 2021 list (5.53 +/- 0.19)e-4 L_sun from Ducrot et al. 2020.

ageGyr.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (st_age); Piaulet-Ghorayeb et al. 2025
ageGyr.note: Same value as Burgasser & Mamajek (2017), who combined many empirical age indicators (colour-magnitude position, density, lithium, gravity features, metallicity, kinematics, rotation, activity). The uncertainty is large.

metallicityFeH.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (st_met); Piaulet-Ghorayeb et al. 2025

spectralType.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (st_spectype); Piaulet-Ghorayeb et al. 2025

vMag.source: Costa et al. 2006 CCD photometry, via SIMBAD
vMag.note: Johnson V. The NASA Exoplanet Archive lists V = 17.02 +/- 0.2 from TICv8, 1.8 mag brighter than this direct measurement; see docs/EXO_TRAPPIST1.md.

jMag.note: 2MASS J (identical to the 2MASS catalogue value in SIMBAD).

kMag.note: 2MASS Ks (identical to the 2MASS catalogue value in SIMBAD).

gaiaDr3Id.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (gaia_dr3_id); confirmed in the Gaia DR3 archive (gaiadr3.gaia_source)

raDeg.note: ICRS. Epoch J2015.5 (the Gaia DR2 epoch carried into TICv8), not J2000: the star moves about 1.03 arcsec per year, so its J2000 position is about 15 arcsec away. Gaia DR3 at epoch J2016.0: RA 346.626522 deg, Dec -5.043528 deg.

decDeg.note: ICRS. Epoch J2015.5 (the Gaia DR2 epoch carried into TICv8), not J2000: the star moves about 1.03 arcsec per year, so its J2000 position is about 15 arcsec away. Gaia DR3 at epoch J2016.0: RA 346.626522 deg, Dec -5.043528 deg.

distancePc.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (sy_dist); Gaia DR2
distancePc.note: 1/parallax from Gaia DR2 (80.451 +/- 0.121 mas). Gaia DR3 measures 80.212 +/- 0.072 mas (12.467 pc); the archive had not adopted it for this star when queried. Light from TRAPPIST-1 takes about 40.5 years to reach us.

inclinationDeg.source: Mean of the seven planets' transit inclinations (NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars; Agol et al. 2021)
inclinationDeg.note: Inclination of the common orbital plane to the plane of the sky (90 deg = edge-on). The seven measured inclinations span 89.728-89.896 deg, so Known Sky draws one shared plane. Transits cannot distinguish i from 180 - i (whether the orbits pass north or south of the stellar centre); we take i < 90 deg.

nodeDeg.source: Fixed choice by Known Sky (no measurement exists)
nodeDeg.note: Position angle of the ascending node on the sky, east of north. Transits constrain only the inclination; how the orbits are turned about our line of sight is unknown. We fix it at 0 deg (node due north). Changing it rotates the whole system about the line of sight and changes nothing seen from Earth.

periodDays.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (pl_orbper); Agol et al. 2021
periodDays.note: The osculating period at the start of Agol et al.'s N-body fit (BJD 2457257.93), not a long-term mean; see inferred.ephemerisPeriodDays for the mean period used to place the planet.

semiMajorAxisAu.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (pl_orbsmax); Agol et al. 2021

radiusEarth.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (pl_rade); Agol et al. 2021

massEarth.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (pl_masse); Agol et al. 2021
massEarth.note: From transit-timing variations (planet-planet tugs), scaled by the stellar mass.

inclinationDeg.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (pl_orbincl); Agol et al. 2021

eccentricity.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (pl_orbeccen); Grimm et al. 2018
eccentricity.note: The default (Agol et al. 2021) parameter set gives no eccentricity, so the archive shows this older transit-timing fit. All seven orbits are nearly circular; Known Sky draws circles.

transitMidBJD.source: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars (pl_tranmid); Ducrot et al. 2020
transitMidBJD.note: A reference transit from an older fit than the period. Paired with the archive period it misses the transit forecast by Agol et al. 2024 nearest 2026-10-11 by -3.0 h (-30 deg of orbit), because that period is an osculating value; Known Sky phases the orbit with the mean ephemeris in inferred.ephemerisTransitMidBJD instead.

equilibriumTempK_A0.source: Computed from the archive's Teff, R* and a, Bond albedo A = 0
equilibriumTempK_A0.note: Teq = Teff * sqrt(R*/(2a)) * (1 - A)^(1/4): the temperature of a uniformly warm planet that re-radiates all absorbed starlight (full heat redistribution, emissivity 1, no greenhouse effect). Real surfaces can be much warmer or colder; uncertainty from first-order propagation of independent errors. JWST measured a 15 um dayside brightness temperature of 490 +/- 17 K (Gillon et al. 2026), as expected for a dark airless rock that does not move heat to its night side. The archive's Ducrot et al. 2020 value is 397.6 K.

equilibriumTempK_A030.source: Computed from the archive's Teff, R* and a, Bond albedo A = 0.3 (Earth-like)
equilibriumTempK_A030.note: Teq = Teff * sqrt(R*/(2a)) * (1 - A)^(1/4): the temperature of a uniformly warm planet that re-radiates all absorbed starlight (full heat redistribution, emissivity 1, no greenhouse effect). Real surfaces can be much warmer or colder; uncertainty from first-order propagation of independent errors.

insolationEarth.source: S = L / a^2 from the archive's luminosity and a
insolationEarth.note: Starlight reaching the planet relative to what Earth receives from the Sun. Agol et al. 2021 list 4.153 (+0.161/-0.159).

densityRelEarth.source: rho = M / R^3 from the archive's mass and radius
densityRelEarth.note: Earth = 1 (5.513 g/cm^3). The archive lists 5.442 g/cm^3. Independent-error propagation overestimates the spread: mass and radius share the stellar-mass uncertainty.

surfaceGravityG.source: g = M / R^2 from the archive's mass and radius

escapeVelocityKms.source: v_esc = 11.186 km/s * sqrt(M / R) from the archive's mass and radius
escapeVelocityKms.note: Scaled from Earth's 11.186 km/s (NASA Earth Fact Sheet).

tidallyLocked.source: Tidal spin-down timescale compared with the system's age
tidallyLocked.note: Not observed. Turbet et al. 2018 find from N-body and tidal modelling that each TRAPPIST-1 planet is likely in synchronous rotation (one face always toward the star). Order-of-magnitude check (Gladman et al. 1996; Q = 100, k2 = 0.3, initial 12 h spin): spin-down in about 60 years, far shorter than the system's 7.6 Gyr age.

ephemerisPeriodDays.source: Mean period: least-squares line through every transit time forecast by Agol et al. 2024 (2015-08-24 to 2027-07-31)
ephemerisPeriodDays.note: The forecast is an N-body fit to transit times measured from the ground, Spitzer, K2, HST and JWST. A straight line cannot follow the planets' mutual tugs (transit-timing variations): the forecast transits stray from it by up to 23 min (8 min rms) over that span. The uncertainty is the formal fit error.

ephemerisTransitMidBJD.source: Mean-ephemeris transit nearest 2026-01-01, from the same least-squares line through the Agol et al. 2024 forecast
ephemerisTransitMidBJD.note: Used with ephemerisPeriodDays to place the planet on its orbit (phase 0 = mid-transit as seen from the Solar System). The uncertainty is the rms of the transit-timing variations about the line. Beyond 2027-07-31 the forecast ends and the error grows slowly.

composition.note: Density 0.99 x Earth's. Agol et al. 2021 find all seven planets consistent with one rocky composition, slightly less iron-rich than Earth (core-mass fraction 21 +/- 4 wt% if water-free; 25 +5/-6 wt% for this planet), or Earth-like rock with added water, or iron-free oxidised rock. The data cannot decide between these. At 4.15 x Earth's insolation it lies beyond the runaway-greenhouse limit, where water could not stay condensed on the surface (Agol et al. 2021).

atmosphere.note: JWST detected the dayside's thermal emission; it is most consistent with little or no atmosphere and no CO2 absorption (Greene et al. 2023). Adding 12.8 um eclipses, an airless fresh-rock surface fits, but so does a hazy CO2 atmosphere (Ducrot et al. 2025); phase curves then strongly disfavoured atmospheres of 1 bar or more (Gillon et al. 2026).

generated.rationale: Insolation 4.15 x Earth's is above the runaway-greenhouse limit, so no surface ice. One of the two scenarios that fit JWST's eclipses is a dark, airless surface of fresh, unweathered ultramafic rock, a hint of recent resurfacing (Ducrot et al. 2025), and JWST phase curves favour an airless, low-albedo rocky surface (Gillon et al. 2026), so we draw dark volcanic plains. Bond albedo 0.05 (rock 0.05, ice 0.45, weighted by ice cover). A faint night-side glow stands for possible tidally driven volcanism. It is kept faint because JWST detected no night-side emission (Gillon et al. 2026).
generated.source: Known Sky rule-based surface generator v1 (inputs: inferred insolation and equilibrium temperature, published JWST constraints)
